projects_en.title: Youki Sun Tracking App
projects_en.description: Helping early risers and afternoon sun seekers find the most beautiful skies.
projects_en.overview:
We've partnered with Youki to design and develop a smartphone app that predicts the quality of sunrises and sunsets before they happen. Drawing on cloud cover, humidity, aerosol density, and sun angle, the app forecasts not just whether a sky will be worth watching, but which colours are likely to appear — helping early risers and afternoon sun seekers find the most beautiful skies.

The design leans into restraint. Sunrises are already beautifully complex; the interface doesn't need to be. Built bilingually in Japanese and English, the app is being tuned to feel calm and considered — a quiet companion for sky-watchers, there at the right moment when the sky is about to do something remarkable.

While picking up the phone is easy for many, for others, it’s an obstacle between them and the help they need. With employee assistance program provider OCP aware of this issue, we suggested that an overhaul of their existing appointment system was necessary to connect as many workers as possible with the support they deserve.

projects_en.title: Zenrise Brand Identity
projects_en.description: Naming, brand identity & collateral design for a Kamakura-based tour agency.
projects_en.overview:
Zenrise is a Japanese tourism company built around discovering the Japan that doesn't announce itself. The identity needed to match that sensibility — understated, bilingual by principle, and respectful of the experience it frames.

The palette draws from the natural environment: moss, sand, and salt-bleached greys. Optima Nova anchors the wordmark; Gill Sans, Yu Gothic & Toppan Bunkyu Mincho handle body copy across both languages. Voice and imagery follow the same logic — sensory over transactional, caught in motion rather than posed.

An identity for a business that believes the best places require a little patience to find.

projects_en.title: OCP Brand Identity
projects_en.description: Rebranding, collateral design & tone of voice for an international health & wellness organisation.
projects_en.overview:
OCP is Oceania's most responsive employee support network, and their brand needed to catch up with who they'd become. The brief was a refresh that felt professional enough to inspire trust, while remaining warm and approachable for anyone reaching out during a difficult moment — a balance that's harder to achieve than it sounds.

The new identity is built around a palette of pale and deep blues, with shades of azure and obsidian providing range across applications. Lighter tones set a calm, welcoming mood; darker shades communicate reliability and strength. The typographic system pairs Transat Text with Europa — clean and modern, with enough authority for a professional context.

The result is a brand that reflects the trust, safety and reassurance OCP brings to workplaces and individuals every day.

articles_en.title: The Future of Retail is Experiential
articles_en.excerpt: It’s no secret that the rise of the internet (and with it, e-commerce) has changed the way people buy things massively, permanently, and arguably very suddenly.
articles_en.body:
It’s no secret that the rise of the internet (and with it, e-commerce) has changed the way people buy things massively, permanently, and arguably very suddenly.

Even the most avid of store-goers have been converted by the superior selection of retailers available online compared to their local city centre, and those in the more recent generations that have grown up with this convenience wonder why their grandpappy insists on trying on his shoes before he buys.

The answer is that grandpappy grew up in an age where trying on his clothes before he bought them wasn’t a luxury and alternative option. Walking into the store, dealing with a sales attendant, and walking out with a paper bag in hand and a wallet $6 lighter for five pairs of socks and a shirt was the only way to purchase your clothing.

Indeed, it was just about the only way to purchase anything. Brylcreem, groceries, a new lawnmower, drinking glasses, or anything else, would’ve involved the same bemoaned ritual. It wasn’t particularly convenient, but it wasn’t particularly inconvenient either — and so bricks and mortar retail arose out of consumer necessity. Stores dotted around the city allowed shoppers a shorter trip to their intended purchase. Retailers focused on organising their stores to make this journey easier — get in, navigate to the aisle that contains your dish soap and garbage bags, and get out.

Today, a lot has stayed the same. Some of the largest retailers in the world follow this exact formula with great success today, although they’ve intelligently pivoted to offer the same (or greater) convenience and selection that they offer in store, online.

However, as we know, a lot has changed. The retailers that have created continued success for themselves today with their online stores, and maintained a large bricks and mortar presence are the retailers we all know, but few of us get excited about. Names (at least in New Zealand) like The Warehouse, as well as international titans like Walmart, Kmart and Target. In these stores, the end product (and its price) are overwhelmingly the largest motivating factors for the purchase. You go to The Warehouse to get a cheap laundry basket — you don’t spend any more time in there than you need to, and your primary goal is to leave the store with a product that works for your purposes and is within your budget.

Many of us breathe a sigh of relief as we exit the electric double doors. We’ve done it. We braved the long checkout lines and the enormity of the store and the products it offers, and we have escaped with our laundry basket secured. Another thing ticked off the eternal to-do list.

Nowadays, physical retail locations like the ones I’ve described above will *never* compete with online stores in essentially every metric that matters from a business perspective. Online stores have lower overheads, and consequentially, lower prices. They also have greater selection, and can be visited on a whim, while the customer is on the couch in their pyjamas. There’s a significant investment associated with creating an online marketplace that really performs, but one that pales in comparison to the fit-out costs of even a single physical location — not to mention the rent each month!

Initially, even based on this short analysis, it looks grim for the physical retailers. In fact, I would hardly hesitate to say that stores that deal in low emotional value commodity items (think rubber gloves, masking tape and our aforementioned laundry basket) that do not create a robust online presence for themselves are doomed to failure in the near future. Retail stores that deal in *important, emotional purchases*, however, have an excellent opportunity to future-proof themselves based on the atmosphere they create in-store.

Instead, now, of thinking of your laundry basket purchase, imagine shopping for a dress or a suit for your wedding. Or maybe a brand-new car — the one you’ve always wanted. Now, we want to take our time. This is important, it’s emotional, and we want to make sure we make the right decision and choose the right thing.

It’s here where bricks and mortar retail that focuses on these more special purchases must distinguish itself — with an experience that even the most polished of online stores cannot offer. Everything from the storefront, what the staff are wearing, the number of products on display, the furniture, the interior lighting, and anything else you could think of play a role in the one trump card a physical store has over an online outfit:

Atmosphere.

With the proper atmosphere, you offer your customer more than just what you’re selling: you offer them a unique experience. One that cannot be replicated online, and preferably one that can’t be replicated down the street at your competitor’s outfit. Your staff and their personalities and expertise — this is something that can never be replicated, especially online. The personal touches and specialities, like offering your customer a coffee, talking with them about their day, or providing feedback to them about their potential purchases are highly valuable and irreplicable parts of the whole experience.

In person, you have the opportunity to engage your customer’s emotions and senses to a far greater degree than you do through their phone screen. They can see your products in the flesh, they can hold them or touch them, maybe they can try them on or be given a demonstration of how they work. They can have their questions answered and their uncertainties allayed — your staff can engage in salesmanship, an opportunity that cannot be exercised online.

More than that, they can sit in the chairs you have chosen, and can look in the mirrors you’ve selected, they can experience the space, walk the floors, and drink in every part of the physical location that you (hopefully) have meticulously created to be a physical representation of your brand. It may make them feel at ease, or maybe it makes them feel important and special. Maybe they get the feeling that your place is high-tech, and so by shopping there they can feel intelligent and forward-thinking. Or maybe your location is decked out with dark ambient lighting, with materials like marble, dark woods & gold — a space designed by the latest and greatest architect in your city. The kind of place they see themselves rewarding themselves at for their hard work, or getting something truly special at.

The point being, that although you can apply the same principles to your online store, there are some parts of the experience of shopping in person that simply cannot be recreated online. By nailing down exactly what you’d like to say about your space, based on the products and/or services that you sell, you can not only justify the existence of a physical location, but begin to utilise it as a truly valuable expression of your business.

By taking what your product, service and/or brand stands for, and exemplifying it in your physical store, you can give your customers an in-person experience that they truly, cannot find anywhere else.

articles_en.title: A Trolley Without Wheels
articles_en.excerpt: Get seen, be remembered, and grow your business. It's time to invest in your customer experience.
articles_en.body:
Imagine life without the humble shopping trolley.

Struggling through the supermarket with your weekly shop spread between measly baskets would be a frequent, almost painful occurrence without these modest innovations. Seemingly simple solutions like trolleys are easily overlooked, but in reality, they hold valuable lessons in building a profitable business.

Experience is the product

Forcing customers to lug their cumbersome groceries through a shop ultimately reduces the amount of food making it past the checkout, limiting the amount of cash entering the tills. The shopping trolley eliminates this problem entirely, encouraging customers to purchase as many groceries as they desire and lining the pockets of supermarket owners everywhere.

Thankfully, for those who don't own a supermarket, this lesson is easily simplified and made effective across any industry: invest in your customer experience to make more money.

A good customer experience is essential in attracting customers, new and old, and encouraging them to spend their cash with your business. A good experience has this effect by making the transaction easier for the customer, consequently encouraging them to return, over and over again.

In the world we live in today, a great customer experience requires more than just a great reputation — but thanks to the glorious notion of design, it's not so difficult to achieve.

The risk of cutting corners

Mistaking design as an optional extra is a common error in the world of business. With the likes of DIY website builders and other digital tools at our disposal, this mistake is becoming endemic across all industries. These digital innovations and your own tenacity to 'learn as you go' may appear to save you a few dollars in the short term, but when functionality issues and bugs begin to arise, DIY design fast becomes more trouble than it's worth.

Design forms the face of your company in the eyes of your customer well before you have the chance to leave a first impression. Whether it's the website that appears in a Google search or the business card passed between friends, these items are the warm host at the door to your business.

Failure to correctly invest in these crucial elements forms barriers between you and your customer, resulting in a poor experience on their end and a constant struggle to obtain new business on yours. Circling back to my supermarket analogy, poor execution of design elements could be likened to offering your customer a trolley without wheels.

Reaping the rewards

Putting the necessary time and effort into the design of your business grants you the privilege of being seen and remembered by your customer for the right reasons.

Investing in these elements also puts you in control of how your business performs amongst your competitors. McKinsey & Company's 2018 *Business Value of Design* study found that the strongest design performers grew revenue 32 percentage points faster than their industry counterparts over a five-year period.

Being seen, heard, and remembered are key factors for growth, all of which are achievable with a great customer experience. That experience begins long before you get on the job — and how your customer perceives your business in the meantime is entirely within your control. Investing in design gives you a vital head start in managing it.

No supermarket would hand a customer a trolley with no wheels on it. Make sure you aren't handing them one either.

Find out where your wheels are missing

We offer a free design audit: an honest assessment of how your website, brand, and collateral are performing as the front door to your business, and where they're quietly costing you work.

articles_en.title: Nobody Likes Being Lied To
articles_en.excerpt: Design decisions are marketing decisions. And the marketing that works best is the kind that takes the customer's side.
articles_en.body:
Where a price sits on a page. Which testimonial gets pulled to the top. What the photography quietly implies about the size of a company. These are design decisions, and they are also marketing decisions, shaping what a customer believes long before they've read a word of the copy.

Design and marketing are usually treated as separate disciplines with separate budgets. In practice, user experience is applied marketing — the point where a company's claims about itself either hold up or come apart under contact with a real person trying to get something done.

Which means design inherits marketing's credibility problem. Marketing has spent decades earning a reputation for making things look better than they are, and every design decision either reinforces that suspicion or works against it.

The assumption underneath the suspicion — that a degree of dishonesty is simply the cost of effective marketing — is wrong. It costs more than it returns, and the evidence on this is not ambiguous.

Nobody likes being lied to

Faced with two comparable products, most people will walk away from the one they feel has been sold to them dishonestly. Not because they've done the maths, but because the sensation of being handled is unpleasant enough to override a small price difference. A business can win the sale and lose the customer in the same moment.

Overselling sets you up to disappoint

When a product doesn't live up to what the marketing promised, the failure isn't only in the delivery. The customer has been taught not to believe the next promise either — and often, not to believe anything else the company puts its name on.

Inflated claims borrow against future business to pay for present business. That works exactly once.

The evidence is not subtle

Edelman's 2026 Brand Trust report found that 88% of people rate trusting a brand as an important or critical factor in deciding to buy from it, putting trust level with quality and value for money. Trust is no longer a soft attribute sitting behind the real decision criteria. It is one of them.

Unless a business sells something people buy exactly once in their lives, it runs on people coming back. Which makes disappointing them a strange thing to build a strategy around.

Taking the customer's side is the commercial position

The usual framing puts user advocacy and commercial interest at opposite ends of a rope — the designer arguing for clarity, the business arguing for conversion. It's a false opposition, and it survives largely because the two sides are being measured over different lengths of time.

Extractive design works, and it rarely looks like lying. Consider the account credit that can only be topped up in denominations which never quite divide into the price of anything worth buying, leaving a small remainder stranded behind every purchase — spendable only in the same place, and only after adding more. Nothing is hidden. No promise is broken. It is simply an arithmetic decision that quietly favours one party, and it reliably lifts the numbers on a quarterly dashboard. That is precisely why these choices are everywhere.

The cost doesn't disappear. It lands later and lands somewhere else, in support load, in churn, and in the reviews a prospective customer reads three years from now.

Designing in the customer's interest and designing in the company's interest are the same decision. The first only looks like a sacrifice on a short enough timeline.

What this means for how we work

Honesty is the centre of how MDMC operates. It is both the clearest difference between us and our competitors and the most useful thing we offer.

Treating design as applied marketing has a practical consequence: every interface, every page, every printed piece is measured against whether it tells the truth about the business behind it. A website that promises a level of polish the service doesn't deliver is not a design success. It is a liability with good typography.

It follows that we work best with businesses that intend to still be here in ten years. Extraction is a strategy with a shelf life, and it isn't one we're equipped to help with. Good work for a business with something genuinely worth saying beats dressing up something that isn't ready. Ogilvy's founding principle still says it best: "only first-class business, and that in a first-class way."

about.headline: We're in it for beautiful, honest, useful work.
about.lede: MDMC is a small team split across Christchurch, Sydney, and Yokohama. We work with founders, operators, and in-house teams on the design problems that don't fit neatly into a brief — the ones that touch product, brand, and operations at the same time.
about.kv_1_body: Branding & identity, digital product design, web & platform design, print & collateral, and the kind of experience design that starts with fixing what's actually broken. We work end-to-end — from diagnosis through to design, build, and beyond.
about.kv_2_body: Two-week loops, no layers between you and the people doing the work. We ask more questions upfront than most, because the right solution usually isn't the obvious one.
about.kv_3_body: Small and medium businesses that have outgrown their current setup, and larger organisations that need an outside eye on how their customers truly experience them. Hospitality, retail, professional services, and anyone whose digital presence no longer reflects the quality of what they do.
about.kv_4_body: Spec work, or projects without a named decision maker. We also never make something we wouldn't want to use ourselves.

about_japan.greeting_title: 「長く、誠実に。」その姿勢で、皆さまと向き合います。
about_japan.greeting_body:
このたびは、MDMC Japanのページをご覧いただき、誠にありがとうございます。

私はニュージーランド出身のディレクターとして、国内外でブランディング、プロダクトデザイン、ウェブサイト制作に携わってまいりました。現在はフィンレイソン ホールディングス ジャパン株式会社（ブランド名:MDMC）として横浜に拠点を構え、バイリンガルチームと共に、日本の企業の皆さまの想いを形にするお手伝いをしております。
私どもが大切にしているのは、お客さまとそのお客さまとの間に、長く続く信頼関係を築くことです。そのためには、製品やサービスそのものの体験を丁寧に見つめ直すことが欠かせません。

デザインや戦略は、企業の姿勢を映す鏡です。消費者の方々を聡明な一人ひとりとして敬意をもって捉え、誠実な仕事を積み重ねることでしか、本当のブランドは育たないと信じております。

国際的な視点と日本のものづくりの繊細さを活かしながら、十年後も価値の続く仕事を、皆さまと一緒に育ててまいりたく存じます。

何卒よろしくお願い申し上げます。

jobs_en.title: Bilingual Administrator
jobs_en.excerpt: Keep the Yokohama studio running — client correspondence, scheduling, and studio administration in Japanese and English.
jobs_en.body:
MDMC Japan is looking for a part-time bilingual administrator to join our Yokohama studio from December 2026. You will be the operational heart of the studio: the person who keeps client correspondence moving, the calendar honest, and the paperwork done properly in both Japanese and English.

Day to day, that means handling correspondence with clients and suppliers in Japanese and English, coordinating meetings across our three studios and their time zones, preparing invoices and quotations, supporting administrative filings, and keeping the studio itself organised and welcoming.
You should have native-level Japanese and confident business English, experience running administration in a small office or studio, and comfort with standard tools for scheduling, documents, and light bookkeeping. Experience with a design or creative business is welcome but not required — care and clarity matter more.

The role is part-time, two to three days per week at our Kitanaka (Bashamichi) office in Yokohama, with some flexibility in which days. Compensation is hourly, set by experience. We expect to welcome the successful candidate around December 2026.

jobs_ja.title: バイリンガル事務スタッフ
jobs_ja.excerpt: 横浜スタジオの運営を支えるポジションです。日英両言語でのお客様対応、スケジュール調整、スタジオの事務全般をお任せします。
jobs_ja.body:
MDMC Japanでは、2026年12月頃から横浜スタジオに加わっていただくパートタイムのバイリンガル事務スタッフを募集しています。お客様とのやり取り、スケジュール管理、書類業務を日本語と英語の両方で丁寧に進めていただく、スタジオ運営の要となるポジションです。
日々の業務は、お客様や取引先との日英での連絡対応、3拠点(クライストチャーチ・シドニー・横浜)の時差をまたぐ会議の調整、請求書や見積書の作成、行政関連の書類のサポート、そしてスタジオを整った心地よい場所に保つことなどです。
ネイティブレベルの日本語とビジネスレベルの英語、小規模なオフィスやスタジオでの事務経験、スケジュール・文書・簡単な経理ツールの基本的な操作に慣れていることを想定しています。デザインやクリエイティブ業界の経験は歓迎しますが、必須ではありません。何より大切なのは、丁寧さと明晰さです。
勤務は週2〜3日のパートタイムで、勤務日はある程度柔軟に相談できます。場所は横浜・北仲(馬車道)のオフィスです。報酬は時給制で、経験に応じて決定します。2026年12月頃の入社を予定しています。
